title: Difficult airway alert wristbands and electronic alerts: recognition of known airway difficulty at the next anaesthetic
subtitle: Retrospective before-after study of the hospital's difficult airway alert system
statement: A teaching hospital introduced a difficult airway alert system in March 2023 (wristband, electronic alert, letter), but it does not know whether known airway difficulty is now recognised before the next airway management, whether unanticipated difficulty has fallen, or whether airway plans change. The hospital's difficult airway database, anaesthetic records and incident reports from 2019 allow a retrospective comparison before and after the change, with the limits that concurrent initiatives impose.
whoAffected: Patients with a known difficult airway (about 1,150 in the hospital's database), anaesthetists and emergency teams who manage their airways later, and the airway committee.
whatHurts: Unrecognised known difficulty leads to repeated intubation attempts, hypoxia and emergency front-of-neck access; an alert system that does not reach the next anaesthetist gives false reassurance.
currentPractice: Since March 2023 patients receive a wristband, an electronic alert and a letter; no evaluation of whether alerts reach the next anaesthetist has been done.
whyNow: The airway committee wants results in March 2027, near-miss reports continue, and a widely quoted national figure cannot be traced.
constraints: No funding; record review by two anaesthetic trainees in protected audit time under the airway lead's supervision. Existing records only; no patient contact. Results to the airway committee in March 2027.
patientCenteredGoal: Every patient with a known difficult airway is recognised and planned for before anyone manages their airway again.
summary: Problem framed as a retrospective before-after evaluation of an alert system, with an untraced national figure to check.
